utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will the Registrar please call the application?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Tribunal has before it an application for deferral by the Federal Republic of Germany in the matter of Dusko Tadic, also known by the names of "Dusan Dule Tadic".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will learned counsel please make their appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I appear as Prosecutor with Mr. Blewitt, the Deputy Prosecutor, and Mr. Niemann, the Senior Prosecuting Attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILKITZKI
utterances.text: I appear as amicus curiae for the Federal Government of Germany of the Federal Ministry of Justice. I am accompanied by a representative of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs and from the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEBITZ
utterances.text: My name is Jorg Sklebitz. I also come as amicus curiae. I am codefender on behalf of the Federal Republic of Germany on behalf of the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will the Prosecutor now present his application?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the aftermath of the horrors of the Second World War, and the trials by the victorious powers of the Nazi leaders at Nuremberg, it was generally anticipated by the international community that a new era had begun. An era in which the human rights of all citizens in all countries of the world would be universally respected. It was not to be. The past five decades have witnessed some of the gravest violations of humanitarian law. Those responsible have too frequently escaped trial and punishment by national courts. Indeed, in many cases they have been in positions of leadership and power in their own countries and they have effectively placed themselves above the law. There was no mechanism devised by the international community for establishing the guilt of perpetrators and punishing them. Justice was denied to millions of victims of murder, disappearances, rape and torture. A catalogue of these gruesome violations of international humanitarian law is to be found in the annual surveys produced year after year by some governmental and inter-governmental agencies and by national and international non-governmental organisations. This Tribunal is the first attempt by the United Nations to enforce international humanitarian law. It is the first recognition of the reality that if international criminal law is to have relevance and is to command respect, it must be capable of enforcement by the international community. This remarkable step by the United Nations is the consequence of events in the former Yugoslavia since January 1991. In describing these events in a provisional order which was granted by the International Court of Justice in The Hague, the judges referred to the words of the General Assembly in a resolution of 11 December 1946 in the context of the Genocide Convention. It was there stated that "the conscious of mankind is shocked by the events and they are contrary to moral law and the spirit and aims of the United Nations". Your Honours, the proceedings today constitute the first public hearing by a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal. The application is brought pursuant to Article 9 of the Security Council Statute which confers upon this Tribunal not only concurrent jurisdiction with all national courts but primacy over them in respect of both the investigation and prosecution of persons whose alleged offences fall within the competence of the Tribunal. In terms of Rule 9, the Prosecutor is given the authority to apply to a Trial Chamber for the issue of a formal request that a national court defer an investigation and prosecution to this Tribunal. In the present case we rely upon the provisions of Rule 9(iii) which provide that such an application may be made by the Prosecutor where in the national investigations or in criminal proceedings instituted in a national court, I quote: "What is in issue is closely related to, or otherwise involves, significant factual or legal questions which may have implications for investigations or prosecutions before the Tribunal". Your Honours, when I took office on 15th August of this year, lawyers and investigators in my Office were already occupied with an investigation into allegations of serious violations of humanitarian law in the Prijedor region of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The allegations came from a number of sources including the report of the United Nations Commission of Experts established pursuant to Security Council resolution 780 of 1992. The Deputy Prosecutor, Mr. Blewitt, became aware of the arrest in Germany of Tadic. The German authorities were subsequently requested to provide the Prosecutor with all relevant information concerning the investigation into crimes allegedly committed by Tadic in Prijedor. The Germany authorities complied with that request and provided my Office with relevant information. In addition, statements have been obtained by my Office from additional witnesses who are presently in the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland. My Office is furthermore in possession of documents relevant to the events in Prijedor and, in particular, the allegations against Tadic. I am presently considering the issue of one or more indictments against individuals who were involved in the serious violations of humanitarian law in Prijedor. As appears from the declaration of Michael Keegan, which is attached to my Application, a policy was executed in Prijedor which involved the widespread and systematic persecution of the non-Serb and, particularly, the Muslim community - a policy which has commonly come to be described as "ethnic cleansing". According to the report of the Commission of Experts, over 43,000 of the approximately 50,000 Muslims who lived in Prijedor in 1991 have left Prijedor or had been killed by June 1993. Witnesses available to the prosecution are able to describe the events which led on 30 April 1992 to the overnight seizure of power in Prijedor by Serbs and the announcements broadcast on local radio to the effect that the area was thenceforth to be called Srpske Opstina Prijedor. Serbian flags were flying on all official buildings and all non-Serbian officials, including policemen, were dismissed. Three major concentration camps (as always they are referred to, logori) were set up in the Prijedor area - in Omarska, a former mine complex, Keraterm, a former ceramics factory, and Trnopolje, a complex of several buildings. At Omarska and Keraterm mostly male members of the non-Serb population of Prijedor were incarcerated - most of them between the ages of 16 and 60. Many leaders and prominent citizens in the non-Serb population were taken to Omarska. Women were generally taken to Trnopolje. The serious atrocities which allegedly were carried out at the three camps are described in some detail in the declaration of Mr. Keegan. They are such that, in our opinion, if they are proved, the persons who ordered the atrocities and those who executed them are guilty of serious violations of humanitarian law and have committed offences which fall within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. I regard it as my duty as Prosecutor to issue indictments against such people if their involvement in these events can be proved by sufficient evidence. The investigations in this regard are still ongoing. I will come now, your Honours, to the case against Tadic. Again, as appears from the declaration of Mr. Keegan, my Office is in possession of witnesses' statements which directly implicate Tadic in some of the atrocities committed in Prijedor. The allegations against him are as follows: He was involved directly in the events which led to the removal of the majority of the Muslim population in Prijedor and, effectively, the destruction of that community. The first of them, according to witnesses, was the organisation of the Serbian referendum in November 1991. Tadic helped create what were, in effect, death lists of Muslim intellectuals and other prominent citizens of Prijedor. He was involved in the forced removals of Muslims from the villages of the Prijedor region and the looting and destruction of Muslim houses. I would emphasise that according to eye-witnesses, when he participated in those events, Tadic wore a military uniform and was, apparently, in command of a group involved in the actions. Again, eye-witnesses are able to testify to Tadic and the group under his command summarily executing unarmed non-Serbs. He was directly involved in directing the transfer of non-Serbs from the villages in the Prijedor region to camps. He was involved in the assaults of prisoners at the camps and at the military barracks in Prijedor. He was seen on numerous occasions in the Trnepolje camp and at Omarska camp. There is an allegation that Tadic was involved in incidents of rape at Omarska and that is being investigated. The gruesome nature of the events which witnesses can describe is illustrated in the following extract from the affidavit -- from the declaration of Mr. Keegan, I quote: “Among the most widely witnessed events that Tadic was involved in was the murder of Emir Karabasic, Jasmin Hrnjic and Enver Alic ... Three prisoners were brutally beaten and tortured by Tadic and others, using metal rods, truncheons, and knives, to the point of unconsciousness. Tadic then forced a fourth prisoner to drink motor oil from the garage and then bite off the testicles of the unconscious prisoners. The prisoners died as a result of their torture". Your Honours, I would also emphasise that Tadic was not a regular official at any of the three camps to which I have referred. It appears that he was in a position of some leadership in the area, in the Prijedor region, and was involved in directing the activities of those with him on his visits to the camps as well as the activities of the regular camp officials. I submit that the evidence of eye-witnesses, if accepted by a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal, will make Tadic guilty of some of the most serious offences falling within the competence and jurisdiction of this international Tribunal. We anticipate that within a short time indictments will be submitted by the Prosecutor to the Registrar against Tadic and other persons who have been identified as having been involved in the "ethnic cleansing" in Prijedor Opstina. In support of such indictments I will rely on the evidence of the witnesses located by the German investigators in Germany and other witnesses who have been located and interviewed by members of the staff of my Office in Germany and elsewhere. The indictments will include serious offences in respect of which the German authorities have no evidence and the other accused will be persons who are outside Germany. It is not possible during this Application, which is in public, to disclose details of the investigations undertaken by my Office, nor is it possible to disclose the identity of other persons under investigation and who are likely to be included in the indictment or indictments which will follow. I can say, however, that the involvement of Tadic in the factual circumstances under investigation by my Office is very significant and it will adversely affect the investigation and prosecution of other individuals if Tadic is prosecuted and brought to trial in Germany. We submit, therefore, that having regard to the scale and nature of the atrocities alleged to have taken place in Prijedor and the relevance of those events in respect of "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this Tribunal is the proper forum (and, we would submit, the only proper forum) for trying those accused (including Tadic) of playing leading roles in respect of those events. It would certainly not be convenient or in the interests of justice if Tadic were to be tried in Germany only to be indicted and again tried in this court. The legal issues which will arise in a trial of Tadic are central to the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. They will involve issues of international humanitarian law which are applicable to the crimes alleged and the nature and manner of their proof. So, both substantive and procedural legal issues which would arise in a trial against Tadic will arise in a case against those who acted in concert with him or acted in pursuance of a common policy. The factual issues speak for themselves. The events in Prijedor during 1992 form an important, a very important, area of investigation by my Office. It follows very clearly, in our submission, that the Tadic investigation by Germany concerns an issue closely related to and involves significant factual or legal questions which will have implications for investigations currently undertaken by me. The Tadic case therefore falls within the provisions of Rule 9(iii) and, in terms of Article 9(2) of the Statute and Rule 10(A), this Chamber may issue a formal request to Germany that its national courts defer to the competence of this Tribunal. Your Honours, until an indictment has been issued against Tadic, a warrant for his arrest cannot be issued under Article 19 of the Statute. However, to the extent that it may be or become necessary, as Prosecutor, I am authorised by Rule 40(i), in a case of urgency, to request any State to arrest a suspect provisionally. I will, therefore, request Germany to effect the provisional arrest of Tadic if that is considered necessary by me for any reason prior to the issue of an indictment. We request, therefore, an order for the deferral by Germany and by the German courts to this Tribunal. Your Honours, the basis of the Application and in the Application that was handed to the Registrar some weeks ago, and in consequence of which this sitting of this Trial Chamber was arranged by the President, the basis was that the German authorities were conducting an ongoing investigation against Tadic. During the course of yesterday, the Press Officer of the Tribunal, Mr. Chartier, brought to the attention of my Office a report from a German press agency, Deutsche Press Agente, to the effect that yesterday Mr. Tadic was, in fact, indicted before a court in Germany. My friend, Mr. Wilkitzki, who appears for the Federal Government in Germany, confirmed the correctness of that allegation this morning. In order to bring the Application correctly within the factual situation, we have prepared an amended Application which records the fact that Tadic was indicted in Germany on 7 November 1994. I beg leave to hand up the new amended Application. (Handed) The relief claimed in the Application is clearly not different in any way from the relief claimed in the original Application. That relief, your Honours, is that the formal request be issued by this Chamber for the deferral of the Tadic proceedings by Germany pursuant to Rule 10 of the Rules and we, accordingly, move for such an order.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have heard your submissions. I have also read the Application and the declaration. I am only intrigued about one issue, that is, the question of the offences for which Tadic was indicted or accused in Germany have been fairly stated in summary, but the offence in Prijedor for which you now are asking for the deferral appears not to have been related to the events for which he was charged in Germany. But, I agree, it comes within subsection 9(iii) where the matters which you claim that they are "related to, or otherwise involves, significant factual or legal questions which may have implications for investigations". I think that ties up with the events which were indicated in Prijedor. But I think, perhaps, one would have liked to know what were the significant facts in the German jurisdiction which raised these allegations or suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the facts on which the German prosecuting authorities have indicted Tadic are clearly not known to us. Until we received the information yesterday, we knew of the investigation by the German authorities and we were grateful (and are grateful) to our colleagues representing and involved in the Tadic investigation in Germany for having given us the factual information which they have against Tadic. We have not investigated (and nor would it be within our competence to investigate) the municipal law of the Federal Republic of Germany under which Tadic can be charged under their municipal law. Our understanding is that certainly one of the charges brought against Tadic is the genocide law of the Republic of Germany which may or may not coincide with the provisions of the International Genocide Convention. But, with respect, if your Honour requires or requests information about the nature of the charges preferred against Tadic, that is a matter which is within the knowledge and competence of our friends representing the Federal Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: President, gentlemen, first of all I would like to make an observation which deals with form, but this will not surprise you, coming from Judge Jorda. Mr. Prosecutor, you have modified or amended your Application. I would like to obtain a French translation of this as French is an official language of the Tribunal. As far as I am concerned, Mr. President, I would rather ask the few questions that I wish to ask once the representative of the Government of the German Federal Republic will have made his statement, and also once the pro bono representative of Dusko Tadic will have spoken as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May we hear the representative of the Federal Government of Germany?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILKITZKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the German Federal Government has demonstrated on several occasions that it will lend its full support, and wishes to lend its full support, to the work of the International Criminal Tribunal and it will continue to do so in so far as this is legally possible. In this connection, it will comply with any requests within that competence made by the Tribunal and its prosecution authority. I base myself on the request for deferral which you have in front of you in its modified form. I would point out also that the relevant German authorities, within the framework of all the duties which are recognised, will transfer all the knowledge gained from the Tadic procedure carried out by the Federal Republic of Germany, and will make this available to the Tribunal. Further requests by the Tribunal will also be complied with in the further continuation of the proceedings in Germany. We will take care that the investigations of the Tribunal should not be adversely affected. Mr. Justice Goldstone has already referred to the events which made the changes yesterday and I may confirm that the Federal General Prosecutor at the Federal Court has instituted proceedings against Tadic. It is my fervent wish to confirm, as it is that of the Federal Prosecutor, that this is in no way intended to disturb or counteract the proceedings of the Tribunal. On the contrary, this act which has been undertaken within the framework of the German Federal procedure, had to be taken in order to secure the facts that Tadic could remain within detention within the German proceedings. The investigating judge at the Federal Court will report in one and a half weeks and decide in one and half weeks time on the continuation of the detention. For this it was necessary that German investigations continued to be conducted with the speediness which is required by the German criminal procedure. I emphasise that this is in no way meant to constitute an obstacle or a reason to believe that the investigations of the German authorities and of the German court would in any way overlap with yours, or that they could affect, adversely affect, the proceedings and the investigations of the Tribunal in any way. The issuing of the order for arrest, which would be necessary in order to secure a transfer, cannot yet be issued according to German law at the present time. Germany has again with the appropriate speediness been preparing a legislative procedure, a Bill, which will lead to the fact, when the relevant authorities have approved this Bill, that such warrant for arrest and a warrant for transfer will be available, so that the duties arising from resolution 827 of the Security Council will be fully complied with. I would point out that we are able to comply with most of the duties arising from this, and further duties arising from this we will be able to comply with when the law has come into effect. In spite of the fact that the legislative period ended in October in the Federal Republic of Germany, nevertheless, on 26 October, just after the start of the legislative period, the Bill was presented by the Government which, if you wish, can be made available to you. It was decided on by the Federal Cabinet -- again this is something new I can tell you today -- last Friday this Bill was put before the Second Chamber of the German Parliament, Bundesrat, with the addition which is possible, according to German Constitutional Law, that this Bill should be regarded as being in need of particular speed so that a shortening of the terms of the legislative procedure is possible. Probably, the Bill will be put to the Bundesrat on 25 November. Then it will be dealt with with all the other authorities, with all the speediness which German law allows. We hope, therefore, that this actually will become effective as soon as possible; then the last obstacle will have been removed which stands in the way of a full compliance with our duties. I would stress that the compliance with the request by the Tribunal, including that which is contained in today's Application, does not raise any legal difficulties for the Federal Government. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any other contributions from the observer? Let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEBITZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, from the point of view of Tadic's defence, I would like to express my position as regards the statements of the Prosecutor as well as those of the representative of the Federal Republic of Germany. First of all, there are no objections on behalf of the defence and Mr. Tadic against a transfer of the deferral of the investigation procedure by the Tribunal in so far as legal conditions can be created in Germany. As regards the individual indictment addressed to Mr. Tadic, I cannot yet express a position except that he contests all the points. A substantive objection is not yet possible because the statement which we received from the Federal Republic of Germany has been much expanded from the warrant which we received in February, and as the defence has not yet had full insight into the documents given to them by the German authorities. Access to documents was allowed in the summer of 1994 and proceedings took place in October 1994. As regards the accusations by the United Nations which are more extensive than what the Federal Republic has alleged, we have not yet received any information and, therefore, we cannot express an opinion as to the various facts of the accusations. But, I would say that there are no objections against the transfer of the proceedings to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, on behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to ask a few questions both to the Prosecutor and to the representative of the German Federal Republic. Perhaps I will first address my questions to Justice Goldstone, the Prosecutor. The first question, which I will expound on: Mr. Prosecutor, you have placed your request on the basis of Article -- of Rule 9. I would like to remind you that -- Article 9, rather, on the basis of primacy over a national court can at any stage of the procedure "formally request national courts to defer to the competence of the International Tribunal in accordance with the present Statute and the Rules of Procedure". So, you have situated your request on that basis, the basis of that Article, which requires that you demonstrate that the object of the procedure followed in Germany against Mr. Dusan Tadic must deal with factual or legal questions which may have implications for the investigation. In the course of your presentation you have, indeed, demonstrated that there were various factual points and points of law. But I would have a few additional questions to ask with relation to what you have said: In the investigations about Prijedor, if I understand what has been said, the Prosecutor's Office has undertaken a series of investigations concerning the facts and events which have taken place in that area of Prijedor. I understand, Mr. Prosecutor, your concern for confidentiality and secrecy with relation to on-going investigations. However, I feel that given the fact that you have based your request on Article 9 rather than Article 8, I believe the Tribunal, since we are in a universal state of law which is the basis justifying our existence, means that we must comply with our own Rules. Thus, concerning Prijedor, I wish first of all to ask a few questions. Again, if you are unable to answer, I will certainly understand, the Tribunal will understand this as well, but I think it is necessary for the purpose of having a clear debate. You have given a series of testimonies which are coded -- I understand this -- but, according to what you have said, they seem to be testimonies made by foreign nationals with relation to the presumed or alleged victims or the country itself. So, are they members of the UNPROFOR Forces, are they members of the United Nations Forces or humanitarian organisations? We do not know. Could you give us clarification? Also, concerning incriminations on the Tadic case, I can understand you cannot give us a determination since this is still in the hands of German justice. I would like to know at present what are the specific incriminations with relation to our brief. Yesterday -- the day before yesterday you publicly mentioned an indictment with a series of charges. I think that it would be good at Tribunal level to be aware of the charges, I am speaking of the full range of these charges, if possible. Again, on Prijedor, since we are dealing with factual issues, I would like to ask you what is the status of the investigations concerning Prijedor, what progress has been made? These questions are directly related to our debate since you need deferral of the Tadic case. I would like to know if Prijedor is in a state of investigation which has reached a point where you do need this or if you are, in fact, at an initial stage of your investigation? In other words, do you need Tadic immediately now at the beginning of your investigation, or is he one of the key components, given the state of progress of your investigation? I think you could give me a reply to this without going into the details, confidential details, of your investigations. I come now to the questions of law, legal questions. You have explained that the legal points, and your demonstration concerning the legal points, are determined because you have explained that problems of international law will certainly occur, both with the Tadic case in Germany and in the Prijedor cases and, thus, the joining of these legal questions authorises you to ask for deferral. So my question is the following: What are these problems of international law? I suppose that for a great part they have to do with jurisdiction or competence, but I believe that for the good deliberation of this court the problems of competence will be posed on a regular basis for all the cases where an application for deferral is made to a given country and, thus, for the Tribunal which will certainly need to supply an answer concerning the questions of competence, I would like to know if you have at the level of the Prosecutor's Office a decision, and I would like to have an answer on this: is it a position of doctrine on the part of the prosecution whenever a foreign country has ratified the creation of this Tribunal, will this be your approach to primacy, so does this constitute your doctrine on primacy? This is relating to Article 9. These are the questions I wanted to ask in relation to this, Mr. Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might deal with the questions you have raised in the order they have been raised. Firstly, the factual questions. The witnesses are almost entirely eyewitnesses, victims who have left the area of the Former Yugoslavia, and who are presently -- obviously the witnesses that the German authorities have made available, their statements have been made available to us, are in Germany -- but the witnesses that are referred to being in the Netherlands, Switzerland and Sweden are, in effect, among the refugee population who were at the time of the alleged atrocities in Prijedor. I referred also to documents which are in our possession which will in due course when the matter comes before a Trial Chamber of the Tribunal, be produced in evidence. So the witnesses are almost entirely persons who will give eyewitness evidence involving the events generally in the Prijedor Opstina, in the Prijedor region, and witnesses who will also give first-hand evidence in relation to specific allegations against Tadic. As far as charges are concerned, we are in a position on the allegations that we already have, on the information we already have against Tadic, would justify, in our submission, bringing an indictment immediately against Tadic on charges of grave breaches of the Geneva Convention, crimes against humanity at least. However, in the view of our Office, it would be more convenient and more proper, indeed more fair to the defence, if all the charges against Tadic were brought in one and the same indictment. For that reason we are of the view that the indictment against Tadic should be brought at the conclusion of the investigations which are well under way. In a moment, with your permission, Mr. President, I will ask Mr. Niemann to reply in more detail to the question relating to the status of the investigation. Before he does that, if I might turn to the legal points, there are a number. One, for example, will be the necessity for the prosecution in respect, certainly, of any charges brought under the grave breaches provisions of the Geneva Convention, to be able to establish that at the relevant time in Prijedor, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a situation of international armed conflict. If at the relevant times there was only an internal armed conflict, then the provisions of the Geneva Conventions would not be relevant to the alleged conduct of Tadic. The interpretation of the international conventions, of customary international humanitarian law which would be relevant, have never received judicial interpretation because until this Tribunal was established there was no competent international Tribunal to consider those matters. There will also be questions of the admissibility of evidence before an international Tribunal. There will be a question also of prejudice, clearly, if the witnesses who are available to the German authorities are to give evidence in a trial against Tadic in Germany and are to be required in respect of the same and additional charges to give evidence before a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal, that clearly would be prejudicial to the proceedings before this Tribunal. So these are some of the legal questions to which I would refer without in any way wishing to suggest that there are not others. There must be many questions of international law and practical questions of evidence and procedure which would be relevant in this regard. I would, with your consent, request Mr. Niemann to be more forthcoming, perhaps, with regard to the present status of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, the position with the investigation at the moment is that it is fairly progressed. The concern that we have is that it becomes necessary for us to formulate the charges we would envisage, not only against Mr. Tadic but against other possible perpetrators in the region. For this reason it is necessary for us to consider the inter-reaction between the various potential offenders. We see Mr. Tadic as being just one party whom we would allege participated in these events. It seems to us that it is more appropriate, if your Honours please, to present an indictment which covers a wider spectrum of the offences that have occurred. It would be, in our submission, unfortunate that Mr. Tadic was not part of that overall proceedings that we would wish to institute. In addition to that, there is the concern that we have about calling the various evidence of armed conflict and so forth that applies in this region which would be pertinent and applicable to Mr. Tadic's case as well as others. It is our submission that the need for consistency is such that it is appropriate that we make this request for deferral. In addition to that, it is finally the interplay between the various potential perpetrators that becomes a matter of considerable importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my friend Mr. Blewitt has pointed out there was one further question that your Honour Judge Jorda put which I did not deal with. That is the question of the policy in respect of requests flowing from the primacy of jurisdiction which this Tribunal is given by the Statute. The policy that we have adopted in my Office is that we certainly do not intend to ask for deferral of all cases before national courts relating to or arising from events in the Former Yugoslavia. Indeed, we have already taken a decision that proceedings which began within the last few days in the Danish courts, we decided was not an appropriate matter to request deferral. The human resources of this Tribunal are such (we only have two Trial Chambers) that we have a limited number of cases which can be expected to be heard by two Trial Chambers. For that reason and, in principle, we have encouraged, and we do encourage, national courts both within the area of the Former Yugoslavia and elsewhere where relevant trials can be brought, to be conducted by national courts. It is in the interests of justice, it is in the interests of this Tribunal that that should be so. However, we regarded that the Tadic case was different certainly to the Danish case and, no doubt, will be different from other cases being investigated both inside and outside the Former Yugoslavia. The Tadic case relates to a specific investigation, an important investigation, which was in any event under way in the Prosecutor's Office. For that reason, there would be an overlap, the allegations against Tadic, the charges to be brought against Tadic, relate directly to potential indictments which will be brought out by the Prosecutor and submitted for confirmation in due course to a judge for confirmation. So, this is not in any way indicative of a policy that would induce us to suggest that there should be a deferment, that primacy should be exercised in any cases, save where there are other principled reasons for such an application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: I would like to say something very briefly, with your permission, Mr. President. Sir, in your submission you have told that presently you are considering to issue one of more indictments against individuals who were involved in the serious violations of humanitarian law committed in Prijedor. According to the declaration of Michael Keegan, a policy which has commonly come to be described as 'ethnic cleansing' was executed in Prijedor. In this connection, it is extremely important to remind that rape has been listed for the first time in the history of humanitarian law as a crime, and that the systematic use of rape has been an essential instrument of ethnic cleansing policy according to the Commission of Experts and numerous human rights groups and organisations. Rape, then, is a crime under the competence of this International Tribunal and, in Prijedor, women were raped. So, it is very important that the indictment you are considering to issue clearly describes all the different elements of the ethnic cleansing policy. There will be no justice unless women are part of that justice, sir. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we share entirely the views which were just expressed by your Honour, Judge Odio Benito. Indeed, in terms of the Statute of the Tribunal reflecting the present state of international humanitarian law, rape is expressly mentioned only in the Article 5, dealing with crimes against humanity. It is our intention, and it is certainly our considered view, that rape is also properly charged under the other provisions of the other Articles of the Statute of the Tribunal. It will certainly be our intention to follow through on that policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me come back again but this is, perhaps, a final one. You have submitted an amended Application. It is in the interests of clarity, better also to indicate the scope of what is sought in the Application, the precise scope of what is being sought, because in the event of the indictment in the German courts, and the position in which Tadic stands there, you will now require proper scope of the Application.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of the Rules, the only order referred to expressly is an order calling for the deferral to the competence of the Tribunal. Rule 10(A) provides that the Trial Chamber may issue a formal request to the State concerned (in this case Germany) that its national court defer to the competence of the Tribunal. We would, respectfully, request an order simply in those terms. We have no doubt, and we would respectfully submit, that if such an order is issued by this Chamber, if in the face of such an order, for example, Tadic was to be brought to trial if a trial actually were to begin in the German courts, in our submission, that would be an act inconsistent with an order for deferral, but whether any detailed order need be issued is a matter which we would, respectfully, submit would be a matter within the competence of this Chamber, of your Honours, to determine. Rule 10(B) refers to a request for deferral, including a request that the results of the investigation and a copy of the court's records (and the judgment if already delivered) be forwarded to the Tribunal. As I have mentioned, and as was confirmed by my friend Mr. Wilkitzki, the German authorities have already, in response to our request, furnished us with the results of the investigations but it may be appropriate to include in the order a request that any further investigations or any further information be transmitted to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe, ladies and gentlemen, that the difficulty is, indeed, related to the change in the last few days of the position of Germany. As a matter of fact, I turn now to the representatives of Germany to ask two factual questions on Tadic and a point of law concerning the legislation. Prior to asking my questions to the German representative, I would like to say that, indeed, for all those who are listening to us, in order to understand thoroughly the meaning of this to make it clear that there is no legal quarrel here which does not have its place in this Chamber. I would like to say that, in any event, the International Tribunal can officially or formally ask national courts to defer at any stage of the procedure. This is a prerogative of the International Tribunal. This being said, I would like to turn to the German Government representative and ask one or two questions. First of all concerning Tadic himself: I believe that this change which occurred in the last few days which, perhaps not coincidental with the holding of this hearing, leads me to ask you what is the present legal standing of that suspect? Until a few days ago he was a suspect who, if I understood correctly, for several months had been kept in provisional custody, if my understanding is correct, and since October the German legal authorities have, in fact, charged him and confirmed their detention order. I would like to ask the representative of the German authorities, because you told us that in fact it was no longer possible to leave him in that situation, but my question is, why were we not made aware of this earlier? Why was this not stated earlier? Why did you not say: "Well, from the point of view of German municipal law, the situation will need to be clarified in the days to come"? What happens is that on 26 October we heard and we learned by way of the press, because you mentioned at length the desire of your country to cooperate with the work of the International Tribunal, but I must say that as far as we are concerned at the Tribunal, we heard that the indictments were being prepared against Tadic, we learned of this by way of the press. The International Tribunal is the guardian of the state of law and I would like to know what the specific situation of Tadic is today with relation to your domestic law. Also I would like to ask a question which is related to the first and has to do with the issue of legislation. You have told us that in the present state of affairs, and I take note of what you said, you told us there were no qualifications or reservations on principle, all at the same time telling us that the legislative bodies of your countries have adopted provisions that would make it possible for the obligations of your country to be fulfilled with regard to this Tribunal. Here again I cannot but make rapprochement with the date of this hearing. Here we are at an International Tribunal created by a resolution dated May 1993 and which has been effectively in operation, even if not function per se, since November, thus one year of operation. What this Tribunal would like to know is the following: What are the practical, legislative or constitutional obstacles that have until now prevented your great country from taking all necessary dispositions in order to comply with the commitments made by Germany with regard to this Tribunal? Quite clearly, I believe everyone here is aware of the fact that this signifies that a delay is going to be brought into the work of the Prosecutor and his Office, as he has demonstrated to us how important the Tadic case is with relation to ongoing investigations. So these are my two questions: one question which relates to the actual status of Tadic today in Germany and, secondly, what dispositions you can take today even if you do not have all the elements in hand, what commitments in principle can you make? Perhaps you could give us a timetable to make it possible for the Tribunal and the international community to have an idea of when this case, which is submitted to the Prosecutor's Office, can find determination at the level of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILKITZKI
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I should like to reply to both questions. As regards the first question, I would like to ask the representative of the General Prosecutor's Office to express his opinion on the general problem of Tadic's status. Nevertheless, I should like to make a few fundamental comments as regards this question as well. I am particularly grateful to Judge Jorda that at the beginning of his comments he said that there is no controversy between the Tribunal and the German authorities. There is nothing further from our minds. At the end of the proceedings it will be as clear as it was at the beginning that we are not just prepared to comply with our duties, but that we are prepared to do everything in our power, as we have done in the past, to help these investigations to achieve success, and that in everything we do we do not intend any interference with the work of the Tribunal. The fact that yesterday this indictment became known has nothing, but really nothing, to do with the timing of today's hearing. The intention of the Federal Prosecutor-General to carry out proceedings with the greatest speediness has been known to us for a long time. We too did not know that by pure coincidence the indictment was to be made yesterday. Strictly legally speaking, it has not been made because it only really is issued when the indictment is notified. The accused will then become indicted and the responsibility will then be transferred to the court from the Federal Prosecutor's Office. Then the court may very well have to decide as regards its own timetable how proceedings will be taken. Meanwhile nothing changes in our own investigations or in your investigations. I would ask you once more to understand that this decision may have been a surprise, but this has been for factual reasons. I must say I also heard about this only today. There is no coincidence whatsoever with today's hearing. As regards the legislative position, I would stress that the Federal Government has not remained inactive since May 1993 and waited for the hearing to be organised, but I would point out that, as has already been discussed in the first debate, the Statute contains a number of new items and entails a number of duties under international law which are something quite unknown for national states and which also requires thorough preparation. In the summer of last year we started to prepare our legislation. Then, as you probably know, there was an encounter of the Member States of the Council of Europe in Strasbourg in September last year, which also was intended clarify the question as to how these duties of international law could be implemented, and all representative Member States at the time came to the conclusion that, because of the fairly concise nature of the Statute, it would be advisable to wait for the issue of the Rules of Procedure before national implementation rules would be issued. This is what we have done. We know that the final wording and text of the Rules of Procedure has only been available since this spring. This again does not mean we have remained inactive since that time. I myself and my Office have presented several revised drafts. In fact, the decision of the Prosecutor to apply for the deferral of the proceedings against Tadic has caused a speeding up as far as we were concerned, in so far as the proceedings which were only intended to be started off after the new legislative period were started off in September with all possible speediness. This was only caused by the Application. Before that I must say we did not have the impression that there was any duty which had to be fulfilled immediately which we could not already comply with. As we have said, in the meantime, as discussed, we have fully complied with a number of requests by the Tribunal. Today I presented to the Prosecutor the statement by the main witnesses in the Tadic case, and we will continue to do so. The only thing we cannot yet do, according to our prevailing law, is the formal transfer of an accused to the court, something which is not required, and also the securing of such a transfer by our own warrant. But this is all balanced out by the fact that in our national law we can fulfil all these requirements in a way (I would stress this) which will have no negative effect on the procedure of this Tribunal. I may perhaps ask Mr. Griesbaum to state the facts on the present situation of Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GRIESBAUM
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecutors, the Federal Prosecutor's Office signed the indictment against Tadic on 3 November. I should like to explain why this time it was chosen and would like to refer to the legal situation in Germany. We have a legal provision that after six months duration of detention, with intervals of three months, the Federal Court will examine the question whether this detention is still justified. Dusko Tadic has been in detention for nine months. In August the first examination by the Supreme Court took place, which decided to continue the detention, but insisted that proceedings and investigations should be conducted speedily. This meant for us that investigations should be concluded, if possible, within the next three months. These three months expire on 18 November. It is unusual in the Federal Republic that such detention without indictment lasts for more than nine months. Indictment is an act which requires much work, much evidence. We have been working for several weeks on this indictment and the fact that it then was concluded on 3 November 1994 is understandable with regard to the expiry of the term on 18 November. We cannot make the indictment just before the end of the expiring term, because the documents have to be sent to the court in Munich. Then these documents are notified and a position has to be taken by the court to the Supreme Court. It is a question of courtesy in the proceedings that the relevant court in Munich, the Bavarian Regional Court in Munich, is given two or three weeks time in order to prepare itself. So, it is a pure coincidence as regards time that this indictment was transferred by us to Munich yesterday. I would ask for the indulgence of the Tribunal. I cannot say anything about the details of the indictment. We have the principle that the public hearing only deals with the points of the indictment once the accused has received the indictment. This has to be translated into Serbo-Croat so that he should not hear through the press what he is being changed with. I would just summarise, we accuse Tadic in 15 cases of genocide; 10 indictments of murder, at least 32 victims and at least seven cases of grave serious bodily harm. That is the extent of the charges brought against him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this concludes the public hearing of the Application. The Trial Chamber will now rise and re-assemble at 2 p.m. prompt for the decision. (The Trial Chamber retired at 11.13 a.m.) 25
